To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

nasal high flow (HF) therapy is effective in improving transcutaneous carbon dioxide partial pressure (PtCO2), and that this improvement is associated with a reduction in the work of breathing in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

nasal high flow (HFNC) therapy reduces transcutaneous partial pressures of carbon dioxide (PtcCO2) in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and that this reduction in PtcCO2 is not associated with any adverse effects on arterial partial pressure of carbon dixode (PaCO2).
nasal high-flow therapy (NHF) reduces hypercapnia in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and that this reduction is associated with a decrease in dyspnoea.

the following questions: Does NHF therapy reduce PtCO2 in patients with COPD?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nasal high flow therapy has been found to be a useful and effective adjunct to standard care in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

the use of nasal high flow therapy in stable COPD is not recommended, as it has not been shown to improve clinical outcomes and there is a lack of evidence regarding its effects on transcutaneous carbon dioxide levels.
the use of nasal high flow in patients with COPD is associated with a significant reduction in transcutaneous carbon dioxide levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of nasal high flow oxygen therapy in COPD patients with hypercapnia and/or hypoxemia may improve their gas exchange, and therefore their clinical outcomes.
nasal high flow (NHF) therapy is an effective method to reduce transcutaneous carbon dioxide levels in COPD patients.
the effects of HFNC in the management of patients with COPD are still unclear and further research is required.
